nh_rainforest_boulder_valley_boulders.blurb: A small cluster of four granite boulders sitting in a hollow inside the Blair Woods section of Pawtuckaway State Park, in southern New Hampshire. Around twenty problems are recorded. The middle of the range is solid, with a good number of V3 and V4 lines, a few easier warm-ups from V0 to V2, and a short list of hard outliers reaching V6 to V8. Because the hollow tends to hold moisture, the stones can stay damp well after rain, so it pays to pick a dry spell. The boulders lie between two better-known blocks, a short walk down a forest trail from the main loop, which makes it an easy add-on to a day among the neighbouring boulders.

nh_lost_ledge.blurb: A slab crag on the eastern stretch of the Kancamagus Highway in the White Mountains. About twenty routes are recorded, mostly trad with a handful of bolted lines and a few top-rope options. Grades run from 5.4 to 5.10, but most of the climbing sits between 5.5 and 5.8, which makes it a comfortable place for newer leaders or for anyone wanting a quiet day. The wall is a warm, sunny slab split into a lower carpet-like section and a larger main slab beside it. Visitors are few. Reaching the base means a woodland walk with a fair bit of uphill, on a path that is not always easy to follow.

nh_slabs.blurb: The slab section of Cannon Cliff, the huge granite face that rises on the west side of Franconia Notch and faces east. About twenty routes are recorded, almost all of them long alpine-style trad lines of several pitches. Most grades fall between 5.6 and 5.9, with a few lines in the 5.10 and 5.11 range and a single much harder outlier. Expect a serious, committing day rather than a quick crag visit: the base is reached over a long talus slope, the rock exfoliates and sheds debris, and storms tend to roll in from the west with little warning. Plan for an early start and a conservative eye on the weather.

nh_middle_sugarloaf_main_face.blurb: A high-angle slab cliff above the Zealand Valley in the White Mountains, visible from US 302 between Bretton Woods and Twin Mountain. Roughly twenty routes are recorded, nearly all of them traditional lines of one to three pitches, plus two easy scrambles. The grades are friendly, from 5.5 up to 5.9, with the heaviest concentration at 5.7 and 5.8. The granite is mostly clean and solid, though a few hollow flakes call for care with protection. A trail of a little over a mile climbs to the ledges above, where the views across the valley make it a pleasant outing for non-climbers in the party too.
